summary: This program stores two playlists as sets of song titles and uses the built-in set operations to find which songs both friends share, the combined list of all songs, and the songs only the first person has.

lines.text: Set is the interface you program against; the concrete HashSet class also lives in java.util, so a complete program needs the line import java.util.HashSet; alongside this one.
The variable is typed as the Set interface while the object is a HashSet, which keeps no duplicates and does not preserve insertion order.
add puts a title into the set; adding the same title twice would simply leave the set unchanged, which is what makes a set the right tool for a collection of unique songs.
The friend's playlist is a second, independent set so the two can be compared.
Passing a set to the HashSet constructor makes a copy, so the operations that follow modify the copy and leave myTitles intact.
retainAll keeps only the elements that also appear in the other set, which leaves exactly the songs both playlists have in common.
The \n prints a blank line first for readability, and the set prints its elements inside square brackets in whatever order HashSet happens to store them.
Another fresh copy of your playlist, this time as the starting point for the union.
addAll merges in every title from the friend's set, and because duplicates are ignored, "Respect" appears only once in the result.
A third copy, because each set operation destroys the set it is applied to.
removeAll strips out every title the friend also has, leaving the songs that are unique to your playlist.
